problem: One science question can get different evidence in Quest chat than in Quest's research chat.
who_has_it: People who ask science questions in Quest chat and in the research chat, and the maintainers who keep both current.
why_it_matters: Two searches mean two sets of sources and two ways of weighing them, so the same question can get different advice, and an improvement to one has to be made again in the other.
why_hard: The research chat's search belongs to the research interface and the evidence service behind the Quest backend, QAR reaches a host's research sources only through declared interfaces, and a host's research search reaches a run only as a retrieval source or a custom tool.
existing_attempts: Web research that reads snippets and then pages, with an answer check that flags claims the turn's reads do not support; a host's research search offered to a run as a retrieval source or a custom tool.

problem: The same request can get a different answer depending on the Quest surface it came from.
who_has_it: People who use Quest in chat, in scheduled tasks and in the apps, and the maintainers who keep each surface current.
why_it_matters: A person who gets two answers to one question cannot tell which to follow, and an improvement made for one surface does not reach the others.
why_hard: Each surface reaches Quest through its own path with its own data, timing and wording, and the differences are easy to add and hard to see.
existing_attempts: Separate handling per surface, and copying changes from one to another by hand.

problem: Each part of QAR can pass its own test while the assistant, as a person meets it across a day, forgets what it knows, acts unasked, claims work it did not do, or answers a vague request with a generic plan, and the person is the one who finds out.
who_has_it: People who use Quest AI as their everyday assistant, and the maintainers who judge it part by part.
why_it_matters: Trust in an assistant is lost by a single surprise: an email described as sent that was not, a delete with no question, an invented address. The person then checks everything it does, which removes the point of having it.
why_hard: The person's seat spans routing, context, planning, acting and answering, so no single part's metric sees the failure; the requirements are many and several, such as nudging unprompted or lasting over sessions, take more than a single message to score.
existing_attempts: Per-part metrics, the chat-quality cases on a dev account, and a small set of day-with-assistant end-to-end cases (a morning briefing, a spoken note, ask-first email and calendar, a background hand-off, a refusal, a delete held for confirmation) scored from the world afterwards and the reply.

problem: What the AI says about the person's own account (which quests exist, what changed, whether a change ran) is re-derived each turn from whatever slice it read, and a change it made is not read back, so within one session it can report the same state two ways, repeat a change it already made, or propose again what it said was done.
who_has_it: People who ask the AI to change their quests and then ask what state they are in.
why_it_matters: In production one account's quests were described as a single completed goal and then as four initialised quests within ten minutes, and the person asked what state the account was in four separate times. An assistant that cannot report its own state is hard to trust with changing it.
why_hard: The host's data changes from many places (the app, other people, background work), a card or cache of it lags, a read on every turn costs time, and a library that serves any host cannot assume one data model.
existing_attempts: A managed card per quest rebuilt on sync, through which a turn is grounded in its quest; live reads through the host's retrieval adapter; the quest change executor and its final-state metric; the answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.
tracking_notes: Proposed in the QAR anatomy review (Mind, Subconscious, Science, World, Body, Higher mind, Overseer).

problem: A general assistant answers from general knowledge. It does not know the person's quests, notes, decisions, past conversations, team or preferences, so its help is plausible but not theirs, and it can state things about their account that are not true.
who_has_it: Anyone asking AI about their own goals and work: Quest users in chat and teams with shared quests.
why_it_matters: Generic help has to be checked and corrected, which costs the time it was meant to save, and confident statements that do not rest on the person's own material erode trust.
why_hard: The relevant material is spread across many sources, far larger than any prompt, changes constantly, differs per person and team, and has to stay inside the scope it belongs to.
existing_attempts: Pasting context into a chat; custom assistants with uploaded files; retrieval products over a single document store; memory features in chat assistants.

problem: Advice and plans are given as one answer, not as the option most likely to work for this person with a metric to check it, and when the better option is unknown the AI does not propose an experiment that would settle it, though the app has an Experiments feature built for that.
who_has_it: People pursuing big goals who need to know what is most likely to work for them, not only what is plausible.
why_it_matters: What sets the product apart from a general chatbot is finding what is most likely to work for the individual and measuring it; an experiment the person carries out gives them a grounded path and the metrics to track it.
why_hard: Most likely needs evidence, the person's own history and a metric, which are rarely all present; an experiment takes the person's time and consent; and a model answers fluently whether or not it has them.
existing_attempts: Experiment tools that find, create and change a quest's experiments when the person asks; experiment generation at the end of quest creation in the host; the intent frame and specification slice for background work.
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: Which AI representative handles a message, a queued task, a newly assigned goal or an autopilot pass is decided in several places by different rules, with no shared definition of the right representative, no labelled measure of how often it is right, and no rule that work spawned from a thread keeps that thread's representative. A quest can have several representatives, each with its own higher mind, so a wrong choice also grounds the request in the wrong view.
who_has_it: People and teams whose quests have more than one AI representative, and anyone who delegates work from a chat or hands a new goal to someone.
why_it_matters: In production a chat's turns ran as the person's default representative while the tasks they spawned ran as two other personas, with a different voice and different evidence in one thread, and the person called the advice inconsistent. Choosing the representative decides whose role, notes and long view ground the work.
why_hard: The fit between a request and a representative depends on roles written in free text, the quests each is assigned and what the person asked for; a bare mention of a name is not the same as asking for it; a representative may be visible to one member of a team and not another; and asking the person each time is its own failure.
existing_attempts: The host's fast-model classifier that picks among a quest's assigned representatives and falls back to the person's default; the task runner's persona resolver; the autopilot roster with per-representative days and instructions; per-viewer visibility of representatives.

problem: The AI answers the request in front of it and lets the person's long-term goal go quiet, so each small task is done without the end in sight; a pointer to the goal in every reply nags, hijacks a simple question or lands on a person who is in a hurry or upset.
who_has_it: Anyone using Quest AI on a quest that serves a larger intent.
why_it_matters: The assistant is meant to keep moving people forward with the end in sight, at the intent level they are working at; an assistant that does not looks like any other chat AI.
why_hard: A pointer is right at one moment and wrong at the next (urgent, narrow, unrelated, emotional, already raised), the right level depends on what the person is doing, and a pointer has to name the real next milestone and the real current reading, not an invented one.
existing_attempts: The reply voice already says to answer first and be proactive only where it is worth the person's time; no measure yet checks whether it points at the next milestone or holds back when it should.

problem: A step only a person on the quest may decide can be taken without them, reach the wrong teammate, or be dropped before they answer.
who_has_it: The person responsible for the account or quest, and teammates asked to approve.
why_it_matters: An irreversible act taken for a person erodes trust and is hard to repair, and an approval request they cannot act on is of no use to them.
why_hard: The model has to recognise a human-only step by judgment, not a word list; the request has to carry enough context to decide; a quest has several people with different roles; and the delivery path differs by host application.
existing_attempts: Confirming everything, denylists of risky words, review queues outside the assistant, and asking in free text.

problem: Replies, experiments and finished work are chosen and judged from the quest alone, not from the top intent and metrics the quest serves, so effort can drift from what the person cares about most and gaps under an intent can go unnoticed.
who_has_it: Anyone with top intents above their quests, and maintainers iterating on a repository's solutions.
why_it_matters: The work done can differ from the work that matters, and the person is not told when an ideal has no solution, a solution has no quest or a metric has no data.
why_hard: The purpose lives in a specification that no prompt used to read, and adding it naively inflates every prompt and charges users who have no intents.
existing_attempts: Life intents specifications, written but read by little that does work; generic standing instructions in deep runs.

problem: Asked how Quest could help, what a feature is for, or whether it is worth it, Quest AI can answer with a list of everything Quest has, or with a generic description, instead of the few features that fit this person's goal and circumstance, or it can assume a circumstance the person did not give.
who_has_it: People new to Quest, including visitors on the free plan, who describe a goal in a sentence and want to know what Quest would do for them.
why_it_matters: These questions help decide whether a person starts using Quest. A reply that leaves them to work out which features matter, or that describes a life they do not have, reads as a brochure and is easy to ignore.
why_hard: The fit needs the goal and circumstance from the message, the features from the documentation, and the judgment to leave out what does not help; a vague goal needs a question first, and a long list looks thorough, so padding is easy and is what a model often writes.
existing_attempts: A feature list written from the documentation, a guide page that lists the questions to ask back for a vague goal, and end-to-end cases that require the reply to name the person's own goal and circumstance and to invent no feature.

problem: Recurring background passes can work when the person's settings say they should not: past the daily budget, on a day outside the roster, or without a cadence being due.
who_has_it: People who set an autopilot cadence and budget for their quest.
why_it_matters: An autopilot that ignores its settings spends money and writes to a quest the person did not ask it to touch, which breaks the promise of the setting.
why_hard: The decision depends on budget, cadence, a pending run-now request, reactive triggers and a roster, and it has to be made before any goal is read or any model is called.
existing_attempts: A cron schedule, a global on or off switch, and per-run checks inside the pass.

problem: Data from one user, team or quest reaches another one's prompt or store, through retrieval, caches, conversation recall, shared stores or the sources fed to the AI.
who_has_it: People whose private notes and decisions could be shown to someone else, and the operators responsible for them.
why_it_matters: A cross-scope leak breaks the promise a personal assistant makes first, and one incident can end a person's trust.
why_hard: Each read path, store and cache has its own scope key, new paths are added often, and a leak is silent: the answer simply contains the wrong person's fact.
existing_attempts: Row-level filters in the database, per-request scope arguments, and review of each new path.

problem: Quest tasks attached to goals can be lost, run twice, or end without an outcome the person sees.
who_has_it: Quest users and teams who delegate research, drafting, checking and follow-up to AI, and the operators who run the worker.
why_it_matters: Delegated work that does not happen, or happens twice, stalls the goals it was meant to move, and people who cannot rely on it stop delegating.
why_hard: Several workers can poll the same queue and claims race, tasks have schedules and representatives, the worker can stop between claim and report, and a task has to be understood in the context of its goal.
existing_attempts: Doing the task by hand in a general chat assistant; scheduled scripts; a single worker; a database claim flag; manual re-queueing.

problem: A person cannot see what their AI is doing for them: whether background work is moving, or what an answer rests on.
who_has_it: People and teammates watching a live chat or a background run, and people who read an answer about their own goals, notes and decisions.
why_it_matters: A silent run looks like a failure, so people interrupt work that was going fine, repeat the request or give up, and a stuck run can go unnoticed. An answer whose path is hidden is harder to trust or correct than the same answer shown with the work behind it.
why_hard: What is shown has to be true to what the run did, so it cannot be invented; the same event stream suits a live viewer, a background milestone feed and a log; the trace of a turn is long and mostly noise; and an explanation a model writes can sound right and be wrong.
existing_attempts: Raw log tailing, spinners, per-step messages and a final summary only; progress sinks that show every event while a person watches and milestones once the run is in the background; interim replies for an attempt that did not meet the goal; the work trace shown beside a reply; linking sources.

problem: A step that needs something from hundreds of the person's records either puts them all in one prompt, which costs more with every entry and buries what matters, or reads a few and misses the rest, and nothing says which record a statement rests on.
who_has_it: Anyone whose notes, insights and logs have grown past what one prompt holds, and every step of Quest AI that is asked something those records answer.
why_it_matters: A statement that cannot be traced to a record cannot be checked, and a cost that grows with the person's history makes the people with the most to draw on the most expensive to help.
why_hard: What bears on a need is not known until the records are read, a model that summarizes can invent a citation, and the same records are asked about again and again with different needs.
existing_attempts: Pasting everything into one prompt; keyword or vector search that returns a few records without reading the rest; one running summary of the collection that serves no particular need.

problem: A request to change a quest leads to changes that were not asked for, to only part of what was asked, or to the same change made twice.
who_has_it: People and teammates who let the AI edit goals, notes and experiments for them.
why_it_matters: Quest data is the person's own plan. An unrequested write is hard to notice and undo, and a partial change leaves the plan inconsistent while the reply claims success.
why_hard: A change request is natural language mapped onto many tools with many arguments; a model tends to be helpful beyond the ask, multi-step requests need each step done once, and a retry after a timeout can repeat a write.
existing_attempts: Tool schemas with explicit arguments, a confirmation step for destructive actions, a scoped writer that performs only the one named operation, and database-level checks of the final state.

problem: Questions about how to use Quest, or what its AI can do for the person, are answered from guesses instead of the product's documentation and actual reach: the AI describes a capability it does not have, or says it cannot do something it can.
who_has_it: New users finding their way around the app, and team members who use only a fraction of its features.
why_it_matters: Guiding a person through the app is one of the AI's largest opportunities: a person who cannot find a feature does not use it, and a person told the AI cannot do something often stops asking. In production one person was told about a submission script that does not exist and two others were told AI work was switched off in their settings when the request could have been done.
why_hard: A usage question has to be told apart from a request to act; the documentation changes with every release; what the AI can reach differs per person, team and deployment, and a model fills a gap in its prompt with a plausible capability.
existing_attempts: The product documentation kept current and included in the chat's context; the message router; tool descriptions with when-to-use text; an answer check that flags claims of unexecuted work.
tracking_notes: Named in a founder's team meeting, 2026-10-27; proposed in the QAR anatomy review.

problem: A message, a goal, a note or a task is attached to a quest by whichever surface received it, each with its own way of picking (the first quest by priority, a word match, an embedding search, a model asked about the quests it was shown), so the same sentence lands on different quests in different places, a quest past the model's window is never offered, and a message no quest fits is given one anyway or none is asked about.
who_has_it: Anyone with more than a handful of quests, which is anyone who uses Quest for more than one goal.
why_it_matters: Work placed on the wrong quest puts unrelated state in front of the AI and unrelated work on the person's plan; a vague nudge such as 'get the store release moving' is only useful if it reaches the quest whose milestones hold it.
why_hard: The words of the message rarely name the quest: the quest is named by its milestones, state and notes, a cue names none of them, two quests share vocabulary, and 'none' is a right answer that a ranker never volunteers.
existing_attempts: A model ordering the quests, each surface prompting its own pick, the first-priority quest as the fallback (each replaced without a measured comparison), then a shared embedding-led ranker and a word-and-meaning ranker with evidence, kept apart.
